title: New focal motor change after head injury
clarityIssues: The later examination is identifiable in the exhibit, but 'for Daniel's later neurologic examination' is awkward: the investigation evaluates a change, not an examination.
Intubation and eye responses add GCS detail without making the unchanged best motor response a consequential competing interpretation in the offered options.

cues.why: Together with unchanged ventilator settings, this explicitly disposes of 'Repeat arterial blood-gas analysis'; a nonmedical reader can see that the offered repeat repeats an already reported measurement.
Only this investigation is labelled urgent, giving it a priority-language advantage in a task asking what to prioritize.

fairness: Urgent CT is the defensible best offered investigation for a confirmed new unilateral deficit after head trauma. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The current question does not meaningfully test the proposed best-GCS trap: none of the choices relies on unchanged best motor response, and the repeat gas is already answered.

This is an offline editorial review of all 19 executable candidate nodes using the specified visible fields; key position and author self-assessments were not treated as evidence. No source verification or clinical approval is claimed. The 18 retirement proposals and one unkeyed BCVI gap are not scored; historical held records are only noted. Existing focal-change holds remain unresolved.
suggestions: Ask which investigation should evaluate the new motor change, and balance urgency language across choices.

Replace the already-completed gas foil with a credible competing assessment at this decision stage. If the unchanged best-GCS construct is retained, make that actual decision error compete with escalation while preserving the focal findings.
Keep the later CT result out of this node; the current sequence correctly does so.

title: Acute subdural evacuation despite preserved responsiveness
fairness: The reported 12 mm acute subdural thickness supports evacuation despite modest shift and retained command following. Observation and ICP-directed medical treatment are credible errors if the learner overweights those reassuring findings, but are not equally good substitutes here.

Interpret the discordant size, shift and examination, then choose operative rather than observational or pressure-directed management. The named diagnosis is appropriate because the task tests management, not diagnosis.

The right-sided collection coheres with left-arm weakness. This node has enough current examination and CT information to stand alone with its case presentation. Earlier feedback prompts structural reassessment but does not supply the evacuation criterion.
Editorial PASS does not resolve the case's carried holds or confer clinician approval.

title: Disposition after negative head CT during apixaban use
clarityIssues: 'There is no additional indication being considered for antithrombotic treatment in this exercise' introduces a medication-treatment issue that none of the choices asks the learner to resolve. It can confuse the existing apixaban indication with the disposition decision.

cues.why: The task partly selects home discharge before comparing it with two admission choices; 'disposition' would be neutral.

cues.phrase: No other injury or medical indication for admission was identified
cues.why: This global admission conclusion risks ruling out both admission options by wording. Necessary observations and home support should remain, but the conclusion should not decide the task.
This is a weak alternative to the genuine routine-repeat-CT misconception; it supplies little resident-level competition in this negative-CT, unchanged-examination scenario.

fairness: The discharge key is defensible for the stated negative CT, baseline examination and reliable home support. The explanation appropriately includes delayed-hemorrhage precautions rather than implying zero risk.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The existing owner hold on this boundary remains unresolved; this review does not adjudicate or remove it.

The normal examination, improving course and support are necessary fairness information, not reasons to remove all reassuring findings. The present construction mostly tests one anticoagulation/disposition rule.
suggestions: Ask which disposition is appropriate and remove the irrelevant sentence about additional antithrombotic indications.

Replace the broad admission-eligibility conclusion with actual findings. Compare plausible disposition strategies and make one supported patient-specific consideration materially affect the routine-admission misconception.
If retained as focused guideline recall, obtain explicit acceptance of that basic educational role instead of calling it a difficult two-step item.

title: Correcting pelvic binder position

cues.why: Directly undermines the only tightening alternative while the exhibit emphasizes a different binder level.

cues.phrase: Remove the binder and continue padded transport
cues.why: In an actively transfused pelvic-ring injury this is an obviously less protective plan, leaving the anatomical correction as the only sensible adjustment.

fairness: The described high binder position supports recentering over the greater trochanters. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The hemodynamic trajectory establishes urgency but does not change the keyed landmark correction: the same answer follows without it. This remains a landmark recall item with a clinical wrapper.
suggestions: Either seek explicit acceptance as a brief safety/technique item or redesign around a genuine mechanical-treatment decision in which position and response both change the action.
Use credible temporary-stabilization alternatives and preserve the necessary anatomical observation; do not obscure the location merely to make the question harder.

title: Pelvic arterial extravasation despite improved pressure
clarityIssues: Pressure during the scan is supplied, but the immediate post-scan trajectory at the treatment decision is less explicit. The distinction matters if a stronger packing-versus-angiography competitor is introduced.

cues.phrase: Pelvic stabilization with serial hemoglobin testing
cues.why: The sequence has already performed binder correction and still reports ongoing transfusion. This choice largely repeats completed support while only the key offers a new targeted bleeding intervention.

cues.phrase: Definitive pelvic fixation as the next intervention
cues.why: Definitive reconstruction is a weak competitor during continuing hemorrhage resuscitation, so the apparent two-step interpretation has little meaningful competition.

fairness: An enlarging arterial contrast focus and continuing transfusion support angiography/embolization among these options. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The returned data are necessary and the sequence is coherent. The node can stand alone with the supplied injury context; prior binder feedback does not give away embolization.
Although the learner can interpret extravasation and consider the response, the options reduce the scored decision to recognition of active arterial bleeding.
suggestions: Replace definitive fixation with a clinically credible competing hemorrhage-control strategy, then supply the current response and workflow facts needed to distinguish it fairly.
Keep actual perfusion and transfusion observations rather than announcing that angiography is feasible or preferred.

title: Persistent neurologic deficit after negative cervical CT

cues.phrase: with multiplanar reconstructions and no motion limitation
cues.why: Directly disposes of 'Repeat cervical CT with reconstructions' by stating that exactly that adequate study is already complete. These adequacy facts are necessary, but the repeat is a spent foil.
A weak next-study alternative during an acute persistent neurologic deficit; the remaining novel study is MRI.

fairness: MRI is the defensible next study for persistent bilateral neurologic findings unexplained by an adequate bony CT. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The observations support cord localization, but the option set permits the simpler rule 'persistent deficit plus negative CT means MRI' without consequential competing interpretation.
suggestions: Retain scan adequacy and the raw neurologic observations; improve the alternatives rather than deleting information needed to establish the CT limitation.
Use a credible competing localization or evaluation pathway that the supplied distribution and course actually distinguish, or accept this explicitly as a basic imaging-safety item.

title: Progressive deficit with cervical cord compression
clarityIssues: The explanation contrasts the MRI with a fracture-negative CT that is not restated in this node. The choice is still answerable independently, but the feedback should remain understandable when this later node is selected alone.

cues.why: Makes continued serial examination the already-failing approach; only decompression actively addresses the reported indentation.
Offers recovery care during active neurologic deterioration, an implausibly premature alternative rather than a difficult resident error.

fairness: Worsening deficits with a persistent compressive lesion support early spine-team decompression. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The sequence is clinically coherent and prior MRI feedback does not prescribe decompression. Current findings are sufficient to answer without the preceding node.
The task asks for a definitive plan, while serial observation and rehabilitation are different care stages; this further narrows the choice without substantive reasoning.
suggestions: Use a neutral treatment-plan task and credible competing spine-management strategies at the same decision stage.
If retaining the progressive emergency presentation, label and seek acceptance of a safety-recognition role; do not manufacture ambiguity by hiding the deterioration.
Restate the relevant earlier CT finding in brief if the explanation continues to rely on it in standalone delivery.

title: Vascular screening after a transverse-foramen fracture
fairness: The fracture location must be translated into arterial risk despite a normal neurologic examination, then into the appropriate vascular imaging modality. Duplex is a credible modality error and cord MRI a credible wrong-target error.
CTA is the best offered screening study. No confident clinical inaccuracy or missing decision-critical fact identified.

The CTA option names more anatomy than its competitors, but arterial imaging is represented in two choices and the stem does not echo carotid/vertebral labels. This is not a convincing knowledge-free key selector.

title: Antithrombotic treatment versus stenting for BCVI
fairness: The learner must interpret the intimal injury and narrowing, then choose treatment while weighing absent bleeding contraindications against absence of an intervention-driving complication. Observation and routine stenting represent consequential errors.
Aspirin is defensible among the offered options. The item does not claim that aspirin is uniquely superior to all other antithrombotic agents; none is offered as a competing key.
The current CTA and bleeding assessment allow standalone answering with the shared presentation. Earlier feedback teaches why to screen but does not supply the treatment choice.

The explanation's 'nonprogressive' is stronger than a single returned CTA establishes, but there is no documented progression requiring intervention. This is a precision issue, not a competing-key defect.
suggestions: For precision, describe the absence of reported progression rather than asserting proven nonprogression from a single study.

title: Abnormal ABI in a perfused injured limb
fairness: The resident must reconcile a warm foot and retained function with abnormal pulse/ABI findings, then distinguish imaging from both observation and immediate exploration.

CTA is the best offered assessment in this stable patient without the supplied hard signs. The ABI value is clearly abnormal rather than a borderline measurement that would make repeat measurement equally defensible.

Listing absent hard signs establishes the imaging-versus-operation boundary; these are necessary clinical observations, not nonmedical wording eliminations. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

title: Reperfusion and stabilization sequence for an ischemic limb
fairness: The resident must recognize the newly threatened but viable limb and reconcile urgent reperfusion with a grossly unstable skeleton. Temporary shunting bridges these competing priorities.

All choices describe actual operative sequences; fixation first delays perfusion, while definitive repair first risks the reconstruction during subsequent skeletal work. Shunting is the defensible best offered sequence under these facts.
Only the key includes three stages, but its additional step is the tested clinical technique rather than explanatory padding; counting stages alone does not establish correctness.

The update explicitly changes the previously warm foot to a cool pulseless foot, so the sequence is coherent. The current CTA, operative control, skeletal instability and viability findings also support standalone delivery. Earlier feedback does not teach shunting.

title: Clinical compartment syndrome with palpable pulses

cues.phrase: Pain rises despite increasing analgesic use
cues.why: Directly marks the analgesia/serial-examination choice as the already-failing plan.
The only urgent treatment competes with continued failed support and another diagnostic delay in an extensively signposted progressive emergency.

fairness: Progressive pain, passive-stretch pain, tense swelling and sensory change after dressing release support immediate fasciotomy; palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

This is an important safety concept, but recognition followed by its standard treatment does not yield two consequential decisions when both alternatives postpone treatment and the examination is so classic.
suggestions: Retain the warning signs and seek explicit safety-recognition acceptance, or redesign the objective around a real assessment-versus-treatment boundary with credible alternatives.

If the task tests the need for pressure confirmation, offer that actual competing plan and make clinical examination reliability explicit; do not weaken emergency findings solely to manufacture difficulty.

title: Persistent symptoms after incomplete leg fasciotomy

cues.why: Almost directly matches 'deep posterior compartment release'; the alternative compartments are explicitly described as soft.

cues.phrase: Anterior, lateral and superficial posterior fascia were opened
cues.why: Combined with 'soleus attachment ... was left intact', the operation note names completed sites and advertises the omitted access. Selecting the only remaining compartment can replace anatomical reasoning.

cues.phrase: Complete the deep posterior compartment release
cues.why: 'Complete' agrees with the narrated omission, whereas the other release repeats already soft, opened compartments.

fairness: Completing an unreleased deep posterior compartment is the defensible answer to the supplied operative record and persistent findings. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The sequence coheres with the preceding fasciotomy decision and contains enough postoperative detail to stand alone. Earlier feedback does not reveal the missing compartment, but this node's own wording does.
Potentially valuable applied surgical anatomy has been reduced to a named-omission and location-matching task.
suggestions: Retain technically accurate operative observations but require interpretation of access and residual muscle/sensory findings rather than repeating the keyed compartment's name in the examination.
Compare plausible corrections at the same operative stage, with clinician-checked anatomy that distinguishes them. Avoid solving the cue merely by replacing anatomical terms with awkward synonyms.

title: Compartment assessment when sedation limits examination
clarityIssues: 'Repeat arterial duplex ultrasound' implies an earlier duplex that the visible record never describes.

cues.why: Names the capability used by 'Serial intracompartmental pressure measurement' and no other option. This is a direct answer-specific availability cue.
Together with the singled-out pressure capability, this rehearses the exact monitoring plan subsequently explained as correct.

fairness: Pressure measurement as an adjunct to serial examinations is defensible in this sedated high-risk patient. The explanation correctly describes supplementation, not a universal isolated pressure cutoff.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The civilian setting can remain if needed to define the intended clinical context; explicitly naming the keyed capability is unnecessary with these alternatives.
After the capability sentence, little remains beyond matching an unreliable examination to the named monitoring tool.
suggestions: Remove the answer-specific capability statement while retaining the setting and ability to perform ongoing observation in neutral terms.
Change 'Repeat' to an initial duplex unless a prior study and its limitations are actually supplied.
Make examination reliability and the evolving findings distinguish credible diagnostic strategies; do not add unsupported pressure thresholds.

title: Persistent pelvic hemorrhage after embolization
clarityIssues: 'Pressure again falls' leaves unclear whether shock persisted continuously through embolization or recurred after a durable response; that chronology affects repeat angiography versus packing.
The record does not state how interval pelvic hematoma enlargement was established at the reassessment.

cues.phrase: Completion runs show no further arterial extravasation
cues.why: Risks making repeat angiography a completed-test foil if read as proof that arterial bleeding can no longer occur, although clinically it is only a time-specific result.

cues.phrase: Definitive internal fixation of the pelvic ring
cues.why: An implausibly definitive reconstruction during recurrent shock; it does not provide a strong third hemorrhage-control competitor.

fairness: Packing is plausible for ongoing nonarterial pelvic hemorrhage after embolization, and inferring the residual source before choosing complementary control is a useful two-step objective.

Uniqueness is not secure: negative completion runs do not exclude a missed, recurrent or newly apparent arterial source during subsequent hypotension. Repeat angiography can remain defensible. This is a clinician-adjudication uncertainty, not a claim that packing is wrong.

The explanation moves from 'can arise' from other sources to a preferred intervention without sufficiently resolving the competing arterial explanation. A negative repeat abdominal ultrasound is helpful but not absolute exclusion of every other bleeding source.
The moderate rating describes the intended source-and-sequence reasoning; unresolved ambiguity should not be counted as hard difficulty.
suggestions: Have Melissa adjudicate the closest alternative and the exact clinical conditions favoring packing over repeat angiography.

Specify the temporal response to embolization, objective ongoing hemorrhage findings and any genuinely decision-critical logistical constraints using supported facts. Do not invent a cutoff or simply label the bleeding venous.
Replace definitive fixation with a credible hemorrhage-control alternative once the intended decision boundary is established.

title: Incomplete cervical CT before collar clearance

cues.phrase: The scan was stopped before the lower cervical levels were acquired
cues.why: Directly supplies the missing-work instruction answered by 'complete cervical CT'; the report repeats the same omission.
The named modality in the presentation further favors completing CT over MRI before the learner has to interpret the clinical context.

fairness: Completing the unacquired anatomy while maintaining the collar is defensible. Unlike an absent export, the acquisition log explicitly proves the anatomy was not scanned; this is a sound fairness distinction.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. However, the duplicated omission plus the named pathway makes this a straightforward completeness check, not two consequential steps.
The shared presentation is needed to identify the hospital's clearance approach. No later completed study should be shown before this decision.
suggestions: Keep one clear acquisition record; remove the redundant restatement of the same missing levels.

Either accept a basic acquisition-safety role or require a meaningful comparison between evidence adequacy and another supported patient consideration. Do not conceal the fact of nonacquisition to force uncertainty.
Review the first explanation together with the second task because it teaches the later CT-clearance rule.

title: Collar removal after adequate negative CT in an obtunded adult

cues.why: The presentation names a 'CT-based clearance pathway', and only the key repeats 'under the CT-based pathway'. This is a direct task/presentation/option wording match.

cues.phrase: The unacquired lower levels prevent use of the high-quality CT clearance pathway
cues.why: The preceding node's explanation teaches the exact missing condition; this node supplies it and asks for the rehearsed consequence.

The quality conclusion plus a second complete-source-review row largely certifies eligibility in advance. Actual acquisition observations are useful; repeated eligibility reassurance adds little inference.

fairness: Collar removal is defensible under the explicitly adopted conditional pathway with the supplied negative adequate CT and no focal discrepancy. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The case is coherent and the current findings stand alone when the shared presentation accompanies it. Without that presentation, the reference to the adopted pathway is incomplete.

After the first explanation, this is protocol recall rather than independent two-step reasoning. The named pathway legitimately limits clinical ambiguity, but its wording need not appear only in the keyed option.
suggestions: Place the adopted pathway in shared context and use parallel plain collar plans without repeating its name only in the key.
Avoid certifying eligibility twice; retain the raw adequacy findings needed for fair application.
Redesign the second node around a distinct consequential discrepancy, or explicitly treat it as scaffolded reinforcement rather than a difficult independent scored objective.

title: Expanding hematoma despite preserved distal pulses
fairness: The resident must recognize expansion beyond marked borders with recurrent bleeding as a hard vascular sign, then choose exploration despite stable systemic pressure and palpable distal pulses.

CTA is a credible competing sequencing error in a stable patient. The single track and lack of associated skeletal injury narrow the localization problem that might otherwise favor preoperative imaging.
Operative exploration is the defensible best answer for this isolated penetrating-injury scenario. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The progression is reported as observations rather than the diagnosis label 'expanding hematoma'; the explanation appropriately supplies that label after answering.

title: Disposition after normal penetrating-limb vascular assessment

cues.phrase: The wound has been cleaned and closed
cues.why: Together with an entirely normal completed assessment, this gives the narrative a discharge-ready ending before the disposition decision.

cues.phrase: Discharge with vascular precautions and scheduled follow-up
cues.why: The key is the longest and only explicitly safety-complete follow-up plan; 'CTA before discharge' omits the same routine discharge safeguards, creating an avoidable completeness advantage.

fairness: The reliable normal examination, normal ABI and lack of an associated admission indication support discharge with follow-up. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The normal examination and ABI are necessary to the disposition rule; they should not be removed to manufacture ambiguity. As written, all findings align and no meaningful competing patient consideration requires a second inference.
This is a useful high-yield counterpart to the abnormal-ABI case, but repetition of the opposite side of one rule does not itself establish resident-level difficulty.
suggestions: Put routine wound care, precautions and follow-up in common context and compare parallel decisions about imaging, admission or discharge.

Introduce a supported, clinically meaningful competing consideration only if it changes interpretation of otherwise reassuring testing; otherwise seek explicit acceptance as focused basic vascular-triage practice.
